episodes.title: Done is a claim
episodes.decision: a loop that stops with `final` has not shown that the change is right. Report "verified" only when a passing check follows the last write; the stop reason (`final` or `step_limit`) is read separately from the check (`notes:93-97`, `:199`). The same rule reads a real session: a final message is a claim until you can cite the observation behind it (`notes:124-129`).

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:04,096
Here is the complete record of an AI agent asked to repair a file.

2
00:00:04,096 --> 00:00:05,151
It read the file.

3
00:00:05,151 --> 00:00:06,268
It wrote the file.

4
00:00:06,268 --> 00:00:09,371
Then it replied: done, and asked for nothing more.

5
00:00:09,717 --> 00:00:11,728
So, is the file repaired?

6
00:00:12,067 --> 00:00:14,143
Nothing in this record can tell us.

7
00:00:14,143 --> 00:00:18,057
By the end of this video, you'll see which observation is missing,

8
00:00:18,057 --> 00:00:21,438
and why an agent saying "done" is a claim, not a verdict.

9
00:00:22,483 --> 00:00:26,494
First, let's separate two things we usually blur together.

10
00:00:26,833 --> 00:00:28,501
A language model produces text.

11
00:00:28,501 --> 00:00:29,524
That's all it does.

12
00:00:29,524 --> 00:00:33,991
Sometimes that text is shaped like a request: call this tool, with these arguments.

13
00:00:33,991 --> 00:00:35,444
We'll call that a proposal.

14
00:00:35,783 --> 00:00:41,315
The program around the model, the controller, decides what happens next.

15
00:00:41,315 --> 00:00:46,463
It checks the call: a tool it knows, the argument names it expects,

16
00:00:46,463 --> 00:00:49,536
a path it allows, and text it can write.

17
00:00:49,536 --> 00:00:52,994
Only then does the proposal become an action.

18
00:00:53,333 --> 00:00:55,955
When a call fails those checks, nothing runs.

19
00:00:55,955 --> 00:00:59,335
The controller sends back a refusal as that call's result,

20
00:00:59,335 --> 00:01:01,607
and the model sees it on its next turn.

21
00:01:01,607 --> 00:01:05,744
The model can ask for anything; the controller decides what is allowed.

22
00:01:06,782 --> 00:01:12,115
Now watch the loop turn by turn, on the smallest task we could think of.

23
00:01:12,115 --> 00:01:15,449
A file, result.txt, contains the number five.

24
00:01:15,449 --> 00:01:17,153
It should contain four.

25
00:01:17,498 --> 00:01:19,807
On turn one, the model calls read.

26
00:01:19,807 --> 00:01:24,083
The controller runs it, and sends back the actual result: five.

27
00:01:24,083 --> 00:01:27,749
Every later request carries it: the file, not a guess.

28
00:01:28,098 --> 00:01:30,538
On turn two, the call is: write four.

29
00:01:30,538 --> 00:01:34,229
The controller writes it, and the tool reports: written.

30
00:01:34,565 --> 00:01:35,647
Should we stop now?

31
00:01:35,647 --> 00:01:36,444
It's tempting.

32
00:01:36,444 --> 00:01:38,038
The file probably says four.

33
00:01:38,038 --> 00:01:40,942
But "written" only tells us a side effect happened.

34
00:01:40,942 --> 00:01:44,016
It doesn't tell us the result meets the specification.

35
00:01:44,365 --> 00:01:46,674
On turn three, the call is: verify.

36
00:01:46,674 --> 00:01:51,094
A fixed check compares the file to the spec, and reports: verified.

37
00:01:51,094 --> 00:01:54,656
That result, under the call's own ID, is the evidence.

38
00:01:54,998 --> 00:02:00,073
On turn four, the model asks for nothing more, so the loop stops with final.

39
00:02:00,073 --> 00:02:03,813
The model proposes, the controller decides, a tool acts,

40
00:02:03,813 --> 00:02:07,152
and the observation goes back for the next choice.

41
00:02:07,152 --> 00:02:09,689
That circle is the core of this agent.

42
00:02:10,732 --> 00:02:13,480
Now rewind, and let the model make a mistake.

43
00:02:13,480 --> 00:02:16,168
On turn two, it writes five instead of four.

44
00:02:16,168 --> 00:02:17,695
The write still succeeds.

45
00:02:17,695 --> 00:02:19,527
The tool still says "written".

46
00:02:19,527 --> 00:02:21,543
Only the check notices: it fails.

47
00:02:21,882 --> 00:02:27,176
Suppose the model now replies with no calls: "Verified." The loop stops with final,

48
00:02:27,176 --> 00:02:28,515
as the contract says.

49
00:02:28,515 --> 00:02:32,534
But that reply cannot change the result under the check's call,

50
00:02:32,534 --> 00:02:35,213
however convincing its explanation sounds.

51
00:02:35,548 --> 00:02:37,872
A message can describe the result.

52
00:02:37,872 --> 00:02:39,718
Only the check observes it.

53
00:02:39,718 --> 00:02:44,639
So report verified only when a passing check comes after the last write.

54
00:02:45,680 --> 00:02:47,172
So how does this loop end?

55
00:02:47,172 --> 00:02:50,731
There are only two stop reasons, and neither one is the check.

56
00:02:51,080 --> 00:02:53,457
Final: a reply had no tool calls.

57
00:02:53,457 --> 00:02:57,345
Step limit: the turn budget, four by default, ran out.

58
00:02:57,345 --> 00:03:01,810
Nothing in the contract detects a repeat, so without a budget,

59
00:03:01,810 --> 00:03:05,411
a model that keeps asking could go around forever.

60
00:03:05,747 --> 00:03:10,449
The check is read separately, from the history: the newest verify result,

61
00:03:10,449 --> 00:03:13,219
or not run, if a later write made it stale.

62
00:03:13,219 --> 00:03:14,636
Here is a run of ours.

63
00:03:14,636 --> 00:03:15,731
The check passed.

64
00:03:15,731 --> 00:03:19,016
Then the model wrote again, and the budget ran out.

65
00:03:19,016 --> 00:03:20,562
Stop reason: step limit.

66
00:03:20,562 --> 00:03:21,528
Check: not run.

67
00:03:21,528 --> 00:03:23,718
The earlier pass no longer counts.

68
00:03:24,063 --> 00:03:27,272
Final means the conversation stopped.

69
00:03:27,272 --> 00:03:29,873
Verified means a check passed.

70
00:03:29,873 --> 00:03:35,337
The two are independent: when we cut the budget to three turns,

71
00:03:35,337 --> 00:03:40,973
the correct run ended at the step limit, with its check verified.

72
00:03:40,973 --> 00:03:43,314
Keep those two words apart.

73
00:03:44,363 --> 00:03:46,208
Now look at the tools.

74
00:03:46,208 --> 00:03:48,473
Each has a narrow contract.

75
00:03:48,473 --> 00:03:50,737
Read takes only result.txt.

76
00:03:50,737 --> 00:03:56,020
Write takes at most thirty-two characters, only for result.txt.

77
00:03:56,020 --> 00:03:59,374
Bash runs only the fixed verify command.

78
00:03:59,713 --> 00:04:04,985
Any other tool, argument name, path or command is refused before any effect,

79
00:04:04,985 --> 00:04:08,454
and the refusal goes back under the call's own ID.

80
00:04:08,454 --> 00:04:13,934
In our run of the fixture's tool function, each of these six came back refused,

81
00:04:13,934 --> 00:04:16,084
and result.txt still held five.

82
00:04:16,430 --> 00:04:19,067
So the name bash does not grant a shell.

83
00:04:19,067 --> 00:04:21,836
That restriction lives in the tool's code;

84
00:04:21,836 --> 00:04:25,858
a prompt asking the model to be careful would not enforce it.

85
00:04:25,858 --> 00:04:27,704
But know this loop's limits.

86
00:04:27,704 --> 00:04:30,737
The turn budget bounds the number of requests.

87
00:04:30,737 --> 00:04:35,220
It does not prove progress, and it is not a secure process boundary.

88
00:04:35,220 --> 00:04:38,780
So run an agent in a dedicated directory or container,

89
00:04:38,780 --> 00:04:41,681
with no employer or cloud credentials in it.

90
00:04:42,730 --> 00:04:46,489
The same question applies to a real agent's instructions.

91
00:04:46,489 --> 00:04:49,061
Some open-source agents publish theirs.

92
00:04:49,061 --> 00:04:53,941
Read them as text, and sort what you find into four kinds: a role or goal,

93
00:04:53,941 --> 00:04:58,821
a tool contract, a stopping or escalation rule, and a request for caution.

94
00:04:59,163 --> 00:05:01,796
Then ask of each one: what enforces this?

95
00:05:01,796 --> 00:05:03,721
A schema, the tool's own code,

96
00:05:03,721 --> 00:05:07,766
or a permission check or sandbox outside the model can enforce.

97
00:05:07,766 --> 00:05:10,398
A sentence that begins "never" only asks.

98
00:05:10,398 --> 00:05:15,213
Our loop makes the same split: the tool's checks before any effect enforce,

99
00:05:15,213 --> 00:05:18,294
while the contract text in the prompt only asks.

100
00:05:18,630 --> 00:05:20,146
Two habits carry over.

101
00:05:20,146 --> 00:05:25,866
A system prompt describes the agent's role and workflow; it does not execute tests.

102
00:05:25,866 --> 00:05:31,516
And for every rule, name the component that enforces it, or say that it only asks.

103
00:05:31,516 --> 00:05:35,306
One limit remains: published files describe components.

104
00:05:35,306 --> 00:05:39,441
Only a captured request can show what one run actually sent.

105
00:05:40,480 --> 00:05:41,649
So let's read one.

106
00:05:41,649 --> 00:05:45,091
This is the sample session that comes with the notes.

107
00:05:45,091 --> 00:05:49,898
It was written by hand, in the format a real recording uses: ten requests,

108
00:05:49,898 --> 00:05:52,691
each with what was sent and what came back.

109
00:05:53,030 --> 00:05:57,104
Request four carries five tool definitions and nine messages:

110
00:05:57,104 --> 00:06:02,513
the system instructions, the user's task, and every earlier call with its result.

111
00:06:02,513 --> 00:06:04,249
The reply holds two calls.

112
00:06:04,249 --> 00:06:06,921
One of them, call six, proposes an edit.

113
00:06:07,263 --> 00:06:12,596
Before you open request five, predict: what will that edit return?

114
00:06:12,596 --> 00:06:13,323
Now look.

115
00:06:13,323 --> 00:06:18,656
Under call six's own ID sits an error: the old text was not found,

116
00:06:18,656 --> 00:06:20,514
and no change was made.

117
00:06:20,863 --> 00:06:25,049
Request six shows the retry, and this time one replacement is made.

118
00:06:25,049 --> 00:06:30,046
Then the agent runs the tests, and request seven carries the result: one failed,

119
00:06:30,046 --> 00:06:30,733
one passed.

120
00:06:30,733 --> 00:06:34,794
Every result is filed under the ID of the call that asked for it.

121
00:06:35,828 --> 00:06:38,648
Now label what you say about this record.

122
00:06:38,648 --> 00:06:42,775
Observed means the record holds it, at a place you can cite.

123
00:06:42,775 --> 00:06:45,870
Request five, message eleven: the error text.

124
00:06:45,870 --> 00:06:47,039
That is observed.

125
00:06:47,378 --> 00:06:52,045
Inferred means you are explaining why it happened, or what comes next.

126
00:06:52,045 --> 00:06:57,444
The model copied a line number out of the file it had read: that is an inference.

127
00:06:57,444 --> 00:07:01,177
The record does hold the agent's own sentence saying so.

128
00:07:01,177 --> 00:07:03,576
That the agent wrote it is observed.

129
00:07:03,576 --> 00:07:06,509
That it is the true cause is still inferred.

130
00:07:06,845 --> 00:07:09,649
Last, find the check behind the final reply.

131
00:07:09,649 --> 00:07:11,752
The final reply says: two passed.

132
00:07:11,752 --> 00:07:13,345
That sentence is a claim.

133
00:07:13,345 --> 00:07:18,633
The observation is in request nine, message twenty-one: exit code zero, two passed.

134
00:07:18,633 --> 00:07:20,736
And it comes after the last edit.

135
00:07:21,078 --> 00:07:23,167
And say what a record cannot show.

136
00:07:23,167 --> 00:07:28,325
This one was written by hand, so it tells you nothing about what a real agent sends.

137
00:07:28,325 --> 00:07:31,150
Your own capture may hide the system messages.

138
00:07:31,150 --> 00:07:35,449
Write that limit down, and never fill the gap from a published prompt.

139
00:07:36,495 --> 00:07:40,306
So, back to where we started: read, write, done.

140
00:07:40,645 --> 00:07:45,459
The missing observation was a passing check after the last write.

141
00:07:45,459 --> 00:07:47,903
With it, you may report verified.

142
00:07:47,903 --> 00:07:50,496
Without it, "done" is just a claim.

143
00:07:50,845 --> 00:07:56,897
This week's assignment ends with one line: accept, narrow, re-check or stop,

144
00:07:56,897 --> 00:07:58,808
and the evidence for it.

145
00:07:58,808 --> 00:08:00,162
So try that here.

146
00:08:00,162 --> 00:08:04,860
A record ends with a write, then "done", and no more calls.

147
00:08:04,860 --> 00:08:07,011
Which claim is unsupported?

148
00:08:07,011 --> 00:08:11,072
Which command would supply the missing observation?

149
00:08:11,072 --> 00:08:14,576
And which of the four words would you write?

episodes.title: Four places to lose a rule
episodes.decision: a plan is complete only when the constraint, its source, its boundary in the code and a case that must be refused all survive from research to verification (`notes:45-47`; `answers:20-22`). A long session is one more place to lose a rule: before a history is shortened, the rule and its source go into a handoff that is checked against the record (`notes:122-126`).

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:02,541
A project proposal contains one rule.

2
00:00:02,541 --> 00:00:07,211
A report may read the reports folder, but it must never write there.

3
00:00:07,550 --> 00:00:11,318
Then someone gives an agent a direct request: add CSV export.

4
00:00:11,318 --> 00:00:15,641
The request does not say where the rule came from, or how to check it.

5
00:00:15,983 --> 00:00:18,021
So here is this week's question.

6
00:00:18,021 --> 00:00:20,887
How does a rule like that survive every step,

7
00:00:20,887 --> 00:00:23,434
from the request to the finished change?

8
00:00:24,483 --> 00:00:28,787
Between that request and a finished change there are four transitions,

9
00:00:28,787 --> 00:00:31,614
and the rule can disappear in any one of them.

10
00:00:31,950 --> 00:00:36,441
Research: the agent reads an old README, but not the current permission test.

11
00:00:36,783 --> 00:00:40,994
Plan: the plan says, add export, and drops the read-only boundary.

12
00:00:41,333 --> 00:00:44,398
Implement: the tool's schema exposes a path,

13
00:00:44,398 --> 00:00:47,184
with no description of the allowed root.

14
00:00:47,533 --> 00:00:50,727
Verify: the test checks that a CSV exists,

15
00:00:50,727 --> 00:00:54,454
but never attempts a write to the reports folder.

16
00:00:54,454 --> 00:00:58,104
And the generated code can still look plausible.

17
00:00:59,150 --> 00:01:02,874
The notes turn this into a check you can do on paper.

18
00:01:02,874 --> 00:01:07,091
Generate: write a one-paragraph plan for the export request.

19
00:01:07,091 --> 00:01:09,620
Verify: underline four things in it.

20
00:01:09,620 --> 00:01:10,674
The constraint.

21
00:01:10,674 --> 00:01:11,447
Its source.

22
00:01:11,447 --> 00:01:13,415
The implementation boundary.

23
00:01:13,415 --> 00:01:14,961
And the negative test.

24
00:01:15,300 --> 00:01:17,809
Here is a plan we wrote for this video.

25
00:01:17,809 --> 00:01:22,957
It reads well enough: add an export command, write the file where the user asks,

26
00:01:22,957 --> 00:01:24,887
and test that the file exists.

27
00:01:24,887 --> 00:01:26,238
Now try to underline.

28
00:01:26,238 --> 00:01:27,911
None of the four is there.

29
00:01:28,250 --> 00:01:29,906
Here is our second draft.

30
00:01:29,906 --> 00:01:31,165
It states the rule.

31
00:01:31,165 --> 00:01:36,200
It names the source: the proposal, and the permission test at this revision.

32
00:01:36,200 --> 00:01:39,844
It sets the boundary: only paths inside the out folder.

33
00:01:39,844 --> 00:01:42,560
And it has one test that must be refused.

34
00:01:42,560 --> 00:01:43,421
Four of four.

35
00:01:43,767 --> 00:01:46,142
If one is missing, the plan is incomplete,

36
00:01:46,142 --> 00:01:48,687
even when the generated code looks plausible.

37
00:01:48,687 --> 00:01:51,458
The rest of this video makes each underline real.

38
00:01:52,500 --> 00:01:57,923
Use three short artifacts rather than one unbounded prompt: research, a plan,

39
00:01:57,923 --> 00:01:59,472
and an implementation.

40
00:01:59,472 --> 00:02:02,642
Research asks: what is true at this revision?

41
00:02:02,642 --> 00:02:07,431
Its artifact is an evidence table, with paths, symbols and unknowns.

42
00:02:07,767 --> 00:02:12,344
Generate: ask for rows that name the export handler and its rejection test.

43
00:02:12,344 --> 00:02:16,128
In this example of ours, the draft comes back with three rows,

44
00:02:16,128 --> 00:02:17,898
and every row says confirmed.

45
00:02:18,233 --> 00:02:22,832
Verify: this export request is invented, so there is no file to open yet.

46
00:02:22,832 --> 00:02:26,045
Every row that said confirmed now says cannot tell.

47
00:02:26,045 --> 00:02:30,203
Later, in the studio, you check the rows against its case checker.

48
00:02:30,203 --> 00:02:33,919
In your own project, you open the file that each row names,

49
00:02:33,919 --> 00:02:36,124
at the revision you are working on.

50
00:02:36,467 --> 00:02:39,546
Mark an unknown explicitly rather than guessing.

51
00:02:39,546 --> 00:02:44,678
A plan is more useful when a reader can disagree with one row and run one check.

52
00:02:45,717 --> 00:02:49,717
The plan asks: what small change would satisfy the request?

53
00:02:49,717 --> 00:02:54,261
Its artifact holds ordered steps, boundaries, and acceptance cases.

54
00:02:54,261 --> 00:02:57,448
Write each case as observable input and output.

55
00:02:57,783 --> 00:02:59,040
The notes give three.

56
00:02:59,040 --> 00:03:03,885
In the first, the request names a file in the out folder, and the rows are valid.

57
00:03:03,885 --> 00:03:07,474
Then the file is created, and the command reports: exported.

58
00:03:07,817 --> 00:03:09,619
The second carries our rule.

59
00:03:09,619 --> 00:03:12,645
The request names a file in the reports folder.

60
00:03:12,645 --> 00:03:17,409
Then no file is written, and the command reports: refused, read-only root.

61
00:03:17,409 --> 00:03:20,628
This case can pass only when something is refused.

62
00:03:20,967 --> 00:03:23,492
In the third, a row is missing its ID.

63
00:03:23,492 --> 00:03:27,878
Again no file is written, and the command reports the invalid row.

64
00:03:27,878 --> 00:03:30,868
A specification that only says, export works,

65
00:03:30,868 --> 00:03:34,258
cannot reveal a missing refusal or a partial write.

66
00:03:35,300 --> 00:03:38,705
Implementation asks: what code expresses that plan?

67
00:03:38,705 --> 00:03:41,510
For an agent, part of that code is a tool.

68
00:03:41,510 --> 00:03:46,117
And a model sees four things about a tool: its name, its description,

69
00:03:46,117 --> 00:03:49,122
its input schema, and the message it returns.

70
00:03:49,122 --> 00:03:50,791
Treat them as a contract.

71
00:03:51,133 --> 00:03:53,948
Read this loose version as a model would.

72
00:03:53,948 --> 00:03:55,526
It writes a CSV report.

73
00:03:55,526 --> 00:03:59,645
Its path is any string, so the model can attempt any string.

74
00:03:59,645 --> 00:04:02,184
Our rule is nowhere in this contract.

75
00:04:02,533 --> 00:04:04,428
Now the revision in the notes.

76
00:04:04,428 --> 00:04:06,511
The name is a verb and an object.

77
00:04:06,511 --> 00:04:10,805
The description states the allowed root and the important exclusion.

78
00:04:10,805 --> 00:04:15,983
And the schema makes the rest machine-checkable: required fields, a closed object,

79
00:04:15,983 --> 00:04:17,624
and a pattern on the path.

80
00:04:17,967 --> 00:04:20,518
Two more checks apply to what comes back.

81
00:04:20,518 --> 00:04:25,435
An error identifies the bad field and the next repair; it is never a traceback.

82
00:04:25,435 --> 00:04:30,538
And a result returns the observation the next decision needs, including a refusal.

83
00:04:31,583 --> 00:04:33,532
Generate: propose two calls.

84
00:04:33,532 --> 00:04:39,167
One names a file in the out folder; the other names a file in the reports folder.

85
00:04:39,167 --> 00:04:42,994
Before you run anything, predict what each will return.

86
00:04:43,333 --> 00:04:47,275
Verify: validate both against the schema, and run the handler.

87
00:04:47,275 --> 00:04:49,690
This is our run of the studio's check.

88
00:04:49,690 --> 00:04:53,504
The first call reaches the handler and comes back: exported.

89
00:04:53,850 --> 00:04:55,813
The second never reaches it.

90
00:04:55,813 --> 00:05:01,070
The path fails the pattern, and the refusal names the field and the repair.

91
00:05:01,070 --> 00:05:04,715
A third call, with an unknown field, is refused too.

92
00:05:04,715 --> 00:05:08,781
Both are rejected before the handler, with no file effect.

93
00:05:09,117 --> 00:05:09,977
One caution.

94
00:05:09,977 --> 00:05:11,983
MCP names a protocol family:

95
00:05:11,983 --> 00:05:16,067
it connects a model application with tools and resources.

96
00:05:16,067 --> 00:05:19,292
The protocol does not make a vague tool safe.

97
00:05:19,292 --> 00:05:22,158
The handler still enforces its boundary,

98
00:05:22,158 --> 00:05:26,888
and the controller still has to pass the result back to the model.

99
00:05:27,933 --> 00:05:30,155
The last transition is verify.

100
00:05:30,155 --> 00:05:35,116
Generate: the smallest function that could satisfy the three cases.

101
00:05:35,116 --> 00:05:36,967
Here is a draft we wrote.

102
00:05:36,967 --> 00:05:41,780
And here is the test a plan without the rule would write: export,

103
00:05:41,780 --> 00:05:43,927
then check that a CSV exists.

104
00:05:43,927 --> 00:05:45,704
On our draft, it passes.

105
00:05:46,050 --> 00:05:50,352
Now run the three cases, each against a fresh temporary directory.

106
00:05:50,352 --> 00:05:51,461
The first passes.

107
00:05:51,461 --> 00:05:54,590
The second fails: the command reported exported,

108
00:05:54,590 --> 00:05:57,327
and a file now sits in the reports folder.

109
00:05:57,327 --> 00:06:02,021
The third fails too: the export crashed, and left a partial file behind.

110
00:06:02,367 --> 00:06:06,216
After a revision that refuses before it writes, all three pass.

111
00:06:06,216 --> 00:06:08,843
The existence test passed on both versions.

112
00:06:08,843 --> 00:06:11,898
Only the two negative cases could tell them apart.

113
00:06:12,233 --> 00:06:15,661
So rerun the acceptance cases after the last write.

114
00:06:15,661 --> 00:06:20,635
And record four things: the command, the exit status, the observed output,

115
00:06:20,635 --> 00:06:21,844
and your decision.

116
00:06:22,883 --> 00:06:27,363
There is one more place to lose a rule, and it is not a transition.

117
00:06:27,363 --> 00:06:29,035
It is the history itself.

118
00:06:29,035 --> 00:06:31,509
A context window is a working budget.

119
00:06:31,509 --> 00:06:35,454
Tool output, repeated reads and failed attempts consume it,

120
00:06:35,454 --> 00:06:39,934
and a later request can then miss the one constraint that mattered.

121
00:06:40,283 --> 00:06:44,831
The notes show this on a second example: one session of nineteen messages,

122
00:06:44,831 --> 00:06:45,814
written by hand.

123
00:06:45,814 --> 00:06:47,719
Its task has a rule of its own.

124
00:06:47,719 --> 00:06:52,574
That rule arrived once, inside an early tool result: do not edit the view file.

125
00:06:52,916 --> 00:06:56,767
A course-written script builds the next request from that history.

126
00:06:56,767 --> 00:07:00,092
Then a short policy, also course-written and not a model,

127
00:07:00,092 --> 00:07:02,659
picks the next edit from that context alone.

128
00:07:02,659 --> 00:07:06,567
In full mode, all nineteen messages are kept, and the check passes.

129
00:07:06,916 --> 00:07:10,126
In auto mode, the older tool results are cleared,

130
00:07:10,126 --> 00:07:12,877
and the line with the rule goes with them.

131
00:07:12,877 --> 00:07:14,188
Now the check fails.

132
00:07:14,188 --> 00:07:16,415
No model was called in either run.

133
00:07:16,415 --> 00:07:20,607
The history got shorter, and the rule was in the part that went.

134
00:07:21,650 --> 00:07:25,029
So before you shorten a history, generate a handoff.

135
00:07:25,029 --> 00:07:29,772
It holds the task, the source of each constraint, the current file state,

136
00:07:29,772 --> 00:07:34,061
the last failed check, what is still unknown, and the next action.

137
00:07:34,400 --> 00:07:35,424
Then verify it.

138
00:07:35,424 --> 00:07:38,499
Compare each line with the recorded messages,

139
00:07:38,499 --> 00:07:41,505
and rerun the check on the current revision.

140
00:07:41,505 --> 00:07:46,971
A summary that says, tests passed, without the tested revision, is not evidence.

141
00:07:47,316 --> 00:07:51,777
And when most entries are stale or contradictory, restart with a written handoff,

142
00:07:51,777 --> 00:07:53,209
and reread the next files.

143
00:07:53,209 --> 00:07:55,467
Compacting is a choice about information.

144
00:07:55,467 --> 00:07:59,487
It is not a guarantee that the model will remember the right information.

145
00:08:00,533 --> 00:08:01,670
Back to our rule.

146
00:08:01,670 --> 00:08:06,152
It survives when every transition keeps it somewhere you can check.

147
00:08:06,152 --> 00:08:09,898
The research names the permission test and its revision.

148
00:08:09,898 --> 00:08:12,574
The plan repeats the read-only boundary.

149
00:08:12,574 --> 00:08:14,648
The schema constrains the path.

150
00:08:14,648 --> 00:08:19,464
And the negative case attempts the write, and expects nothing to change.

151
00:08:19,800 --> 00:08:23,220
This week's project proposal asks for the core scenario,

152
00:08:23,220 --> 00:08:26,152
a scope boundary and your first observable case.

153
00:08:26,152 --> 00:08:31,222
The studio goes further: three to five cases that can fail, kept with the proposal,

154
00:08:31,222 --> 00:08:32,933
and one tighter tool schema.

155
00:08:32,933 --> 00:08:37,331
Finish with one line: accept, narrow, recheck or stop, and its evidence.

156
00:08:37,666 --> 00:08:38,645
So try it now.

157
00:08:38,645 --> 00:08:41,579
A later plan omits the read-only boundary.

158
00:08:41,579 --> 00:08:44,234
Which research artifact would you add?

159
00:08:44,234 --> 00:08:47,797
And which negative case, before any implementation?

episodes.title: The near miss
episodes.decision: a skill's description is ready when three requests that should trigger it and one near miss behave as you predicted, in a run you saved. A structure check does not show that: it reads two files and cannot observe which skill an agent selected.

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:03,683
Here is the description of one skill.

2
00:00:03,683 --> 00:00:06,371
And here are four requests.

3
00:00:06,717 --> 00:00:08,571
Three of them should trigger the skill.

4
00:00:08,571 --> 00:00:09,808
One should leave it quiet.

5
00:00:10,150 --> 00:00:10,658
Which one?

6
00:00:10,658 --> 00:00:12,841
And how would you show that you were right?

7
00:00:13,883 --> 00:00:15,138
Start without an agent.

8
00:00:15,138 --> 00:00:18,083
Suppose a project has a release check that you repeat.

9
00:00:18,083 --> 00:00:20,974
Before you write a skill for it, run it once by hand.

10
00:00:21,317 --> 00:00:22,288
Three commands.

11
00:00:22,288 --> 00:00:25,915
The first tells you whether unrelated edits are present.

12
00:00:25,915 --> 00:00:28,311
The second catches whitespace errors.

13
00:00:28,311 --> 00:00:30,448
The third is the project's check.

14
00:00:30,783 --> 00:00:33,249
Note the revision, and keep the output.

15
00:00:33,249 --> 00:00:36,537
If the check fails, write the failure down and stop.

16
00:00:36,537 --> 00:00:38,434
Do not hide it behind a skill.

17
00:00:39,483 --> 00:00:41,147
Now encode the procedure.

18
00:00:41,147 --> 00:00:44,275
A skill is a directory with a skill file in it.

19
00:00:44,275 --> 00:00:48,534
The front matter names the skill, and describes when it applies.

20
00:00:48,883 --> 00:00:50,954
The body explains three things.

21
00:00:50,954 --> 00:00:52,558
Steps name the commands.

22
00:00:52,558 --> 00:00:55,565
Judgement states at least one stop or branch.

23
00:00:55,565 --> 00:00:59,774
Verification names the exact check, and the evidence it leaves.

24
00:01:00,816 --> 00:01:05,002
Set the skill beside your hand run, and compare them line by line.

25
00:01:05,002 --> 00:01:06,143
Which step is new?

26
00:01:06,143 --> 00:01:07,919
Which evidence is preserved?

27
00:01:07,919 --> 00:01:11,787
And which decision would be impossible from the output alone?

28
00:01:12,133 --> 00:01:15,409
One thing the skill does not add is permission.

29
00:01:15,409 --> 00:01:19,104
It is a workflow description, not a permission grant.

30
00:01:19,104 --> 00:01:20,847
It can suggest a command.

31
00:01:20,847 --> 00:01:26,424
The shell, the repository's policy and your review still decide whether it runs.

32
00:01:27,466 --> 00:01:30,860
Which part of the file is on hand when a request arrives?

33
00:01:30,860 --> 00:01:33,719
Only the metadata: the name and the description.

34
00:01:33,719 --> 00:01:36,637
They are available before the skill is activated.

35
00:01:36,983 --> 00:01:42,187
The body is loaded after selection, and bundled resources only when they are needed.

36
00:01:42,187 --> 00:01:44,914
So the description is the selection surface.

37
00:01:45,249 --> 00:01:50,099
A long explanation there makes unrelated requests look like matches.

38
00:01:50,099 --> 00:01:53,380
A vague description makes the skill invisible.

39
00:01:53,716 --> 00:01:56,653
So say what the skill does, and when it applies.

40
00:01:56,653 --> 00:01:59,407
Then treat selection as a claim, and test it.

41
00:02:00,449 --> 00:02:05,279
The course kit has a complete example: a skill for researching a codebase.

42
00:02:05,279 --> 00:02:06,976
Read only its description.

43
00:02:06,976 --> 00:02:11,152
Its job is to record existing handlers, tests and request paths,

44
00:02:11,152 --> 00:02:12,588
with source locations,

45
00:02:12,588 --> 00:02:17,940
when you need a fact-only map of an unfamiliar codebase before proposing a change.

46
00:02:18,282 --> 00:02:22,108
Now predict, before you look at its trigger record.

47
00:02:22,108 --> 00:02:26,758
Trace this request, and cite the files and lines you observed.

48
00:02:26,758 --> 00:02:30,133
Trigger: it asks for a read-only path record.

49
00:02:30,482 --> 00:02:34,648
Tell me what the handlers and tests do, before we discuss edits.

50
00:02:34,648 --> 00:02:37,967
Trigger: it asks for current facts before a change.

51
00:02:37,967 --> 00:02:42,003
Build a read-only call-path record for this unfamiliar module.

52
00:02:42,003 --> 00:02:45,973
Trigger: it names the same bounded research job in new words.

53
00:02:46,316 --> 00:02:50,288
And the fourth: implement the change, and add a regression test.

54
00:02:50,288 --> 00:02:50,971
Stay quiet.

55
00:02:50,971 --> 00:02:52,647
It asks for implementation.

56
00:02:53,681 --> 00:02:56,051
That fourth request is the near miss.

57
00:02:56,051 --> 00:03:00,343
It is close: the description ends just before a change is proposed,

58
00:03:00,343 --> 00:03:02,841
and this request asks to implement one.

59
00:03:02,841 --> 00:03:06,812
But the skill is for a fact-only map, so it should stay quiet.

60
00:03:07,148 --> 00:03:10,506
And if it does stay quiet, that is not a failure.

61
00:03:10,506 --> 00:03:12,287
It is the expected result.

62
00:03:12,287 --> 00:03:15,919
Keep the prediction and the observation side by side.

63
00:03:16,265 --> 00:03:19,056
The three that should trigger have a rule too.

64
00:03:19,056 --> 00:03:21,847
They test the description in natural language.

65
00:03:21,847 --> 00:03:26,156
A request that just names the skill does not count as one of the three.

66
00:03:27,198 --> 00:03:29,354
Now open the trigger record.

67
00:03:29,354 --> 00:03:31,742
Every request has three fields.

68
00:03:31,742 --> 00:03:34,976
Should trigger is the boundary you intend.

69
00:03:34,976 --> 00:03:38,519
Predicted is what you expected before the run.

70
00:03:38,519 --> 00:03:42,369
Observed is what the command line actually showed.

71
00:03:42,715 --> 00:03:46,069
In the kit's record the three agree on every request.

72
00:03:46,069 --> 00:03:47,587
But read the first line.

73
00:03:47,587 --> 00:03:50,751
This is a synthetic example written by the course.

74
00:03:50,751 --> 00:03:53,726
No classmate and no agent session was observed.

75
00:03:54,065 --> 00:03:57,957
So in this file, observed marks where an observation goes.

76
00:03:57,957 --> 00:03:58,897
It is not one.

77
00:03:58,897 --> 00:04:03,796
Label the record synthetic in your notes, and never describe it as a run.

78
00:04:04,831 --> 00:04:07,569
The course supplies a checker for these two files.

79
00:04:07,569 --> 00:04:11,401
It checks the front matter and the directory name, the three sections,

80
00:04:11,401 --> 00:04:13,591
and the record: four to twelve requests,

81
00:04:13,591 --> 00:04:16,876
at least three that should trigger without naming the skill,

82
00:04:16,876 --> 00:04:18,682
and at least one that should not.

83
00:04:19,031 --> 00:04:21,924
Here is our run on the kit's skill and its record.

84
00:04:21,924 --> 00:04:24,642
Structure checked, and the exit status is zero.

85
00:04:24,981 --> 00:04:30,529
The lines above it are advice: the words each request shares with the description.

86
00:04:30,529 --> 00:04:32,559
The near miss shares one word.

87
00:04:32,559 --> 00:04:33,032
Change.

88
00:04:34,081 --> 00:04:36,361
But look at what that run passed.

89
00:04:36,361 --> 00:04:39,332
A record in which nobody observed anything.

90
00:04:39,681 --> 00:04:42,040
The checker reads files only.

91
00:04:42,040 --> 00:04:47,652
It runs no model, so it cannot observe which skill an agent selected.

92
00:04:47,998 --> 00:04:53,188
So a passing structure check is not evidence that an agent selected the skill.

93
00:04:53,188 --> 00:04:55,849
Do not report its output as a model run.

94
00:04:56,898 --> 00:05:00,181
The observation has to come from a run of your own.

95
00:05:00,181 --> 00:05:04,237
Run your coding agent's command line once, on a fixed revision.

96
00:05:04,237 --> 00:05:08,229
Save the exact request, copied before the run, and the output.

97
00:05:08,565 --> 00:05:10,763
Set observed to true or false,

98
00:05:10,763 --> 00:05:15,967
and only from the selection evidence the command line actually reports.

99
00:05:15,967 --> 00:05:21,024
If it shows no selection, write selection not shown in your run file,

100
00:05:21,024 --> 00:05:23,736
and explain the basis for each value.

101
00:05:24,081 --> 00:05:28,668
Save the rest as well: the revision, the exact verification command and its result,

102
00:05:28,668 --> 00:05:31,375
and the boundary, meaning the files that changed.

103
00:05:31,375 --> 00:05:33,972
Then another reader can identify what happened.

104
00:05:34,315 --> 00:05:38,095
And run the agent in a dedicated directory or container,

105
00:05:38,095 --> 00:05:41,065
with no employer or cloud credentials in it.

106
00:05:41,065 --> 00:05:45,926
Never put a key in a prompt, a screenshot, a transcript or a repository.

107
00:05:46,965 --> 00:05:50,005
What if your run disagrees with your prediction?

108
00:05:50,005 --> 00:05:53,552
A mismatch is evidence about the description's boundary.

109
00:05:53,552 --> 00:05:57,099
Keep it, describe the description change under revision,

110
00:05:57,099 --> 00:05:59,696
and recheck only the mismatched requests.

111
00:06:00,031 --> 00:06:01,778
Suppose the near miss triggered.

112
00:06:01,778 --> 00:06:05,764
We made that one edit in a copy of the kit's record, and ran the checker.

113
00:06:05,764 --> 00:06:08,002
One problem: a mismatch needs a revision.

114
00:06:08,348 --> 00:06:11,381
The tempting repair sets observed back to false.

115
00:06:11,381 --> 00:06:12,392
We ran that too.

116
00:06:12,392 --> 00:06:13,530
Structure checked.

117
00:06:13,530 --> 00:06:16,879
The checker cannot see that the record was rewritten.

118
00:06:17,215 --> 00:06:21,107
The honest repair keeps the observation and adds a revision,

119
00:06:21,107 --> 00:06:23,377
with a recheck of that one request.

120
00:06:23,377 --> 00:06:24,934
Structure checked again.

121
00:06:24,934 --> 00:06:28,826
Keep both outcomes in your record, the failure and the pass.

122
00:06:29,165 --> 00:06:30,378
Both records pass.

123
00:06:30,378 --> 00:06:33,278
Only the run you saved can tell them apart.

124
00:06:33,278 --> 00:06:37,256
So compare every observed value with your saved transcript.

125
00:06:38,298 --> 00:06:40,291
So: run the workflow by hand.

126
00:06:40,291 --> 00:06:41,734
Encode it as a skill.

127
00:06:41,734 --> 00:06:44,552
Predict three triggers and one near miss.

128
00:06:44,552 --> 00:06:47,851
Run once, and save what the command line showed.

129
00:06:47,851 --> 00:06:50,669
Then compare prediction with observation.

130
00:06:51,014 --> 00:06:54,848
End with one decision line: accept, narrow, recheck or stop,

131
00:06:54,848 --> 00:06:57,532
followed by the evidence that supports it.

132
00:06:57,532 --> 00:07:00,599
A passing structure check can go in that record.

133
00:07:00,599 --> 00:07:03,985
It does not prove that the agent selected your skill.

134
00:07:04,331 --> 00:07:06,077
One question to take with you.

135
00:07:06,077 --> 00:07:09,919
What is the nearest request that should stay quiet for your skill?

136
00:07:09,919 --> 00:07:11,782
Write it down before you submit.

episodes.title: A request or a gate
episodes.decision: leave a rule as a request only if skipping it is acceptable. Otherwise add a testable hook or a human review step for it, and keep one blocked and one passing record. The film shows this on the course hook and one staged change: an unused import is stopped before the commit, the fixed file passes, and each record is labelled with what it proves and what it leaves open. The shorter second half applies the same reading to a subagent: a role is a contract (an instruction, a small tool allowlist and a required hand-back), and a hand-back is a proposal until you open what it cites.

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:01,935
An agent is fixing a parser.

2
00:00:01,935 --> 00:00:06,356
The repository has an instruction file, and one rule in it says:

3
00:00:06,356 --> 00:00:09,811
do not change dependency files in a parser change.

4
00:00:10,150 --> 00:00:12,046
Suppose the agent is in a hurry.

5
00:00:12,046 --> 00:00:15,601
It stages the parser, and the lockfile with it, and commits.

6
00:00:15,950 --> 00:00:19,963
The rule was written down, and the commit went through anyway.

7
00:00:19,963 --> 00:00:24,041
So for every rule you write, ask: is this a request, or a gate?

8
00:00:25,082 --> 00:00:28,115
Start from a failure, then write the rule.

9
00:00:28,115 --> 00:00:31,798
"Be careful" is a request with no observable check.

10
00:00:31,798 --> 00:00:37,213
Write the rule as a sentence an agent can act on, and a person can inspect.

11
00:00:37,549 --> 00:00:41,665
A useful rule predicts a failure, and names evidence that can check it.

12
00:00:41,665 --> 00:00:45,433
The failure: a commit changes the lockfile while fixing a parser.

13
00:00:45,433 --> 00:00:48,274
The rule: no dependency files in a parser change.

14
00:00:48,274 --> 00:00:51,520
The evidence: the staged path list contains no lockfile.

15
00:00:51,866 --> 00:00:53,445
Two more from the notes.

16
00:00:53,445 --> 00:00:58,579
The command changes without its regression test; so for every behavior change,

17
00:00:58,579 --> 00:01:01,080
name the test that tells old from new.

18
00:01:01,080 --> 00:01:04,503
And a generated command writes outside the checkout;

19
00:01:04,503 --> 00:01:09,637
so stay below the repository root, and stop and ask when a path is outside it.

20
00:01:10,682 --> 00:01:14,761
Rules like these go in an instruction file at the repository root.

21
00:01:14,761 --> 00:01:19,272
A good entry names the scope, the allowed command, the expected evidence,

22
00:01:19,272 --> 00:01:20,693
and the stop condition.

23
00:01:21,032 --> 00:01:23,572
Now read it the way a hurried agent would.

24
00:01:23,572 --> 00:01:26,656
The request to run the parser tests can be skipped.

25
00:01:26,656 --> 00:01:29,257
The stop rule can be checked by a reviewer,

26
00:01:29,257 --> 00:01:32,643
but it is still an instruction until a gate enforces it.

27
00:01:32,982 --> 00:01:37,126
An instruction file gives context, and a decision procedure.

28
00:01:37,126 --> 00:01:41,753
By itself, it does not make the filesystem or Git refuse an action.

29
00:01:42,799 --> 00:01:47,607
A request is a message to the agent: run the focused test, and report the output.

30
00:01:47,607 --> 00:01:49,210
The agent may leave it out.

31
00:01:49,549 --> 00:01:54,212
A gate is attached to an event the repository controls: before a commit,

32
00:01:54,212 --> 00:01:57,385
refuse staged Python files with an unused import.

33
00:01:57,385 --> 00:02:01,400
Git invokes the hook, even when the agent forgets the request.

34
00:02:01,749 --> 00:02:04,061
So a hook is a narrow invariant.

35
00:02:04,061 --> 00:02:07,600
It is not a replacement for tests, or for review.

36
00:02:08,648 --> 00:02:11,154
The course hook is a short Python file.

37
00:02:11,154 --> 00:02:12,824
Read it before you use it.

38
00:02:12,824 --> 00:02:18,219
A small wrapper in the Git hooks folder hands it the staged path list, as one event.

39
00:02:18,565 --> 00:02:20,002
It checks two things.

40
00:02:20,002 --> 00:02:24,448
No protected file may be staged, and the lockfile is one of them.

41
00:02:24,448 --> 00:02:28,416
And no staged Python file may import a name it never uses.

42
00:02:28,765 --> 00:02:31,013
It reads and parses each file.

43
00:02:31,013 --> 00:02:33,186
It never imports or runs one.

44
00:02:33,186 --> 00:02:38,656
For a finding it exits with two, and for a clean list it exits with zero.

45
00:02:39,698 --> 00:02:44,047
Now try the gate, in a disposable copy of your repository,

46
00:02:44,047 --> 00:02:47,271
with no credentials or employer data in it.

47
00:02:47,271 --> 00:02:53,269
The generated proposal: add an import the file never uses, stage it, and commit.

48
00:02:53,615 --> 00:02:54,541
Predict first.

49
00:02:54,541 --> 00:02:58,706
The hook should stop this commit, because the import is unused.

50
00:02:59,048 --> 00:03:00,530
In our run, it does.

51
00:03:00,530 --> 00:03:05,938
The hook names the file, the line and the unused import, and prints stop.

52
00:03:05,938 --> 00:03:11,419
It exits with two, Git reports a nonzero status, and no commit is created.

53
00:03:11,765 --> 00:03:14,408
Save that output as your blocked record.

54
00:03:14,408 --> 00:03:16,720
And if the commit had gone through?

55
00:03:16,720 --> 00:03:19,033
Then stop, and inspect the wrapper.

56
00:03:19,033 --> 00:03:22,336
Do not rewrite the record to make it look blocked.

57
00:03:23,381 --> 00:03:24,151
Now verify.

58
00:03:24,151 --> 00:03:29,472
Read the hook's output, remove the import, stage the file again, and commit.

59
00:03:29,814 --> 00:03:33,167
This time the hook prints pass, and exits with zero.

60
00:03:33,167 --> 00:03:34,585
The commit is created.

61
00:03:34,931 --> 00:03:37,350
Save that as your passing record.

62
00:03:37,350 --> 00:03:42,262
Then ask Git to show the commit, to confirm which files entered it.

63
00:03:43,297 --> 00:03:46,372
Keep both records, and label what each one proves.

64
00:03:46,372 --> 00:03:50,923
The blocked run proves that Git presented these staged paths to this hook,

65
00:03:50,923 --> 00:03:53,628
and that the hook returned a nonzero status.

66
00:03:53,964 --> 00:03:56,380
That is evidence that the gate fired.

67
00:03:56,380 --> 00:03:59,775
It is not evidence that the final change is correct.

68
00:04:00,114 --> 00:04:05,958
The passing run proves only that this input satisfied the hook's narrow checks.

69
00:04:05,958 --> 00:04:09,435
The application's behavior is still unverified.

70
00:04:09,435 --> 00:04:13,725
So run the focused test, and inspect the diff, separately.

71
00:04:14,064 --> 00:04:17,841
A common mistake is to record only the passing commit.

72
00:04:17,841 --> 00:04:21,408
The first record shows the gate stopped that input.

73
00:04:21,408 --> 00:04:24,136
The second shows the clean path passed.

74
00:04:24,136 --> 00:04:24,835
Keep both.

75
00:04:25,881 --> 00:04:28,288
So where does that leave the instruction file?

76
00:04:28,288 --> 00:04:31,532
Treating an instruction as a permission boundary is a mistake.

77
00:04:31,881 --> 00:04:35,643
For an invariant, add a testable hook, or a human review step.

78
00:04:35,643 --> 00:04:38,132
And keep the request, for useful context.

79
00:04:39,181 --> 00:04:41,049
Here is our way to choose.

80
00:04:41,049 --> 00:04:45,072
For each rule, ask what happens when the agent skips it.

81
00:04:45,414 --> 00:04:47,795
If that is acceptable, leave it as a request.

82
00:04:47,795 --> 00:04:49,647
If it is not, give the rule a gate,

83
00:04:49,647 --> 00:04:52,345
and keep one blocked and one passing record for it.

84
00:04:53,381 --> 00:04:57,571
The same thinking applies when you hand work to a subagent.

85
00:04:57,571 --> 00:05:00,768
A role is more than a label such as reviewer.

86
00:05:00,768 --> 00:05:06,592
Give the subagent its own instruction, its own tools, and its own output contract.

87
00:05:06,931 --> 00:05:10,165
For a bounded parser change, the notes use three roles.

88
00:05:10,165 --> 00:05:14,223
A researcher locates the parser and its callers, and changes nothing.

89
00:05:14,223 --> 00:05:16,987
An implementer changes only the named function.

90
00:05:16,987 --> 00:05:21,222
A reviewer judges the issue, the diff and the evidence, without editing.

91
00:05:21,564 --> 00:05:26,176
After each hand-back, the parent agent, or a person, chooses whether to continue.

92
00:05:26,176 --> 00:05:30,275
The subagent cannot enlarge its allowlist, declare its own work correct,

93
00:05:30,275 --> 00:05:32,495
or silently replace a missing artifact.

94
00:05:33,531 --> 00:05:36,971
And a generated hand-back is still a proposal.

95
00:05:36,971 --> 00:05:39,663
Ask a researcher to find the parser.

96
00:05:39,663 --> 00:05:44,001
If the hand-back names no file and no function, reject it.

97
00:05:44,001 --> 00:05:47,142
Ask for the bounded report again, or stop.

98
00:05:47,481 --> 00:05:52,600
If it does name them, open every cited location, run the stated check,

99
00:05:52,600 --> 00:05:55,892
and record what the check does not establish.

100
00:05:56,231 --> 00:06:00,127
A hand-back is evidence only for the fields it names.

101
00:06:00,127 --> 00:06:03,875
Mark each claim confirmed, refuted, or cannot tell.

102
00:06:03,875 --> 00:06:06,522
An unsupported claim is cannot tell.

103
00:06:07,564 --> 00:06:10,157
Then pass on only what the next role needs.

104
00:06:10,157 --> 00:06:13,775
The implementer gets the research note, and the named files.

105
00:06:14,114 --> 00:06:19,084
The reviewer gets the issue, the diff and the test evidence, in a fresh context.

106
00:06:19,084 --> 00:06:23,805
So it can check the contract, instead of trusting the implementer's summary.

107
00:06:24,147 --> 00:06:27,306
A fresh context makes the contract visible.

108
00:06:27,306 --> 00:06:30,318
It does not make the reviewer infallible.

109
00:06:31,363 --> 00:06:34,742
So: write each rule from the failure it prevents.

110
00:06:34,742 --> 00:06:36,466
A request can be skipped.

111
00:06:36,466 --> 00:06:39,776
A gate sits on an event the repository controls,

112
00:06:39,776 --> 00:06:44,534
and you keep the record of it blocking, and the record of it passing.

113
00:06:44,880 --> 00:06:49,843
End your record with one decision line: accept, narrow, recheck or stop,

114
00:06:49,843 --> 00:06:51,566
with the evidence for it.

115
00:06:51,566 --> 00:06:56,047
A clean hook run can support accepting the staged-path invariant.

116
00:06:56,047 --> 00:07:00,045
It cannot support accepting untested application behavior.

117
00:07:00,045 --> 00:07:03,836
And bring the same instruction file, and the same gate,

118
00:07:03,836 --> 00:07:06,731
to your project's technical specification.

119
00:07:07,080 --> 00:07:08,542
One question to try.

120
00:07:08,542 --> 00:07:11,831
A hook prints a finding, but exits with zero.

121
00:07:11,831 --> 00:07:13,512
Did it gate the commit?

122
00:07:13,512 --> 00:07:15,851
And what observation settles it?

episodes.title: Is it ready for an agent?
episodes.decision: score a repository's readiness only from an anchor you observed at a named revision. A tidier tree with no changed observation does not raise the score.

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:02,638
Here is a small task for a coding agent.

2
00:00:02,638 --> 00:00:06,133
This status function strips its input, lowercases it,

3
00:00:06,133 --> 00:00:08,639
and walks through three if statements.

4
00:00:08,639 --> 00:00:11,211
Replace the conditionals with a lookup.

5
00:00:11,550 --> 00:00:17,689
A proposal comes back: one table, one line, and no if statements at all.

6
00:00:17,689 --> 00:00:19,138
It looks cleaner.

7
00:00:19,138 --> 00:00:20,161
Is it right?

8
00:00:20,500 --> 00:00:24,393
The task also says what to preserve: whitespace handling, case,

9
00:00:24,393 --> 00:00:25,938
and the unknown fallback.

10
00:00:25,938 --> 00:00:26,989
But in this file,

11
00:00:26,989 --> 00:00:31,191
neither that contract nor the caller is written beside the function.

12
00:00:32,232 --> 00:00:36,008
Before you judge the proposal, look at what will judge it.

13
00:00:36,008 --> 00:00:38,938
The fixture's verifier holds ten fixed cases.

14
00:00:38,938 --> 00:00:42,323
Each one is an input, and the label it must produce.

15
00:00:42,665 --> 00:00:43,651
Predict a few.

16
00:00:43,651 --> 00:00:45,340
Plain "ok" gives passed.

17
00:00:45,340 --> 00:00:47,170
Capital "OK" gives passed.

18
00:00:47,170 --> 00:00:50,549
"ok" with a space on each side gives passed too.

19
00:00:50,549 --> 00:00:55,476
And "pending" is not a status the function knows, so it gives unknown.

20
00:00:55,815 --> 00:00:59,233
The same ten cases run against every version of the function.

21
00:00:59,233 --> 00:01:00,354
The code may change.

22
00:01:00,354 --> 00:01:01,306
The cases do not.

23
00:01:02,349 --> 00:01:04,463
Run the ten cases on the proposal.

24
00:01:04,463 --> 00:01:05,148
Seven pass.

25
00:01:05,148 --> 00:01:08,320
Three fail, and the verifier exits with status one.

26
00:01:08,665 --> 00:01:12,600
The failures are the padded inputs: "ok" with spaces,

27
00:01:12,600 --> 00:01:17,352
"fail" with a tab and a newline, and capital "PASS" with spaces.

28
00:01:17,352 --> 00:01:19,356
The proposal dropped strip.

29
00:01:19,699 --> 00:01:23,932
For each of them, the original function returned the right label.

30
00:01:23,932 --> 00:01:25,821
The proposal returns unknown.

31
00:01:25,821 --> 00:01:29,990
A caller that sends a padded status would see its result change.

32
00:01:31,031 --> 00:01:35,892
The worked refactor uses the same table, and keeps strip in front of lower.

33
00:01:35,892 --> 00:01:39,002
All ten cases pass, and the verifier exits zero.

34
00:01:39,348 --> 00:01:42,476
Now count the if statements: three in the original,

35
00:01:42,476 --> 00:01:44,562
and zero in both shorter versions.

36
00:01:44,562 --> 00:01:48,119
The count cannot tell the broken one from the working one.

37
00:01:48,465 --> 00:01:52,039
A shorter function still has to keep the contract.

38
00:01:52,039 --> 00:01:55,471
And ten of ten establishes those ten cases only.

39
00:01:55,471 --> 00:01:58,902
It does not prove the behavior for every string,

40
00:01:58,902 --> 00:02:01,476
or that a caller accepts the change.

41
00:02:02,515 --> 00:02:04,489
One step came before those runs.

42
00:02:04,489 --> 00:02:07,203
You ask for one bounded expression, as text.

43
00:02:07,203 --> 00:02:10,966
What comes back is text too, until a person has inspected it.

44
00:02:11,315 --> 00:02:12,605
So read it first.

45
00:02:12,605 --> 00:02:15,641
Only then copy it into a candidate file.

46
00:02:15,641 --> 00:02:21,486
Nothing executes the reply itself: the ten cases meet the file you inspected.

47
00:02:21,831 --> 00:02:24,762
And if the text asks for more, such as a key,

48
00:02:24,762 --> 00:02:28,084
network access or an install you do not know, stop.

49
00:02:28,084 --> 00:02:32,448
Run a generated command only in a dedicated directory or container,

50
00:02:32,448 --> 00:02:34,402
one that holds no credentials.

51
00:02:34,402 --> 00:02:37,202
Otherwise, record the missing prerequisite.

52
00:02:38,248 --> 00:02:42,671
Suppose the text you copied into the candidate file was this instead:

53
00:02:42,671 --> 00:02:45,619
a conditional expression, and no table at all.

54
00:02:45,965 --> 00:02:47,569
Run the ten cases on it.

55
00:02:47,569 --> 00:02:48,438
All ten pass.

56
00:02:48,438 --> 00:02:52,982
And the if count is zero, because the verifier counts if statements,

57
00:02:52,982 --> 00:02:55,656
and a conditional expression is not one.

58
00:02:55,998 --> 00:02:59,335
But the task asked for a lookup, and there isn't one.

59
00:02:59,335 --> 00:03:04,182
The count is a narrow measure: it cannot see what replaced the if statements.

60
00:03:04,182 --> 00:03:05,253
So open the file.

61
00:03:05,253 --> 00:03:10,289
A refactor is not accepted until the requested structure has been inspected too.

62
00:03:11,331 --> 00:03:15,695
Now run the same ten cases on the function you started with.

63
00:03:15,695 --> 00:03:16,495
Ten of ten.

64
00:03:16,495 --> 00:03:17,222
Exit zero.

65
00:03:17,564 --> 00:03:21,434
So the original and the refactor both pass every case.

66
00:03:21,434 --> 00:03:24,516
Only the if count differs: three, and zero.

67
00:03:24,516 --> 00:03:27,095
The cases cannot tell the two apart.

68
00:03:27,431 --> 00:03:28,954
And that is the point.

69
00:03:28,954 --> 00:03:30,823
The behavior was preserved.

70
00:03:30,823 --> 00:03:34,562
What changed is how much a fresh session has to guess.

71
00:03:34,898 --> 00:03:39,857
In the original, a session must infer the contract from a chain of conditionals.

72
00:03:39,857 --> 00:03:40,849
In the refactor,

73
00:03:40,849 --> 00:03:45,189
the lookup table and the fallback are visible beside the change point.

74
00:03:46,231 --> 00:03:49,408
Scale that up from one function to a repository.

75
00:03:49,408 --> 00:03:52,652
A prepared repository also names its entry point,

76
00:03:52,652 --> 00:03:56,358
its contract and its offline check in its context files.

77
00:03:56,358 --> 00:03:59,668
The agent still needs permission to read and edit.

78
00:03:59,668 --> 00:04:03,242
The repository has only removed the avoidable guesses.

79
00:04:03,581 --> 00:04:05,500
That is what agent-ready means.

80
00:04:05,500 --> 00:04:09,772
A fresh session can find the relevant code, learn the local contract,

81
00:04:09,772 --> 00:04:12,992
run a short check, and report what it did not check.

82
00:04:13,331 --> 00:04:17,482
And readiness is a property of evidence at a named revision.

83
00:04:17,482 --> 00:04:20,942
It is not a feeling about how tidy the tree looks.

84
00:04:21,981 --> 00:04:24,493
So what can a comparison like this show?

85
00:04:24,493 --> 00:04:28,826
The fixture is one function, so it cannot show every kind of blocker.

86
00:04:28,826 --> 00:04:32,657
On a whole repository, you record observations like this one:

87
00:04:32,657 --> 00:04:36,112
the documented check exits zero on the refactored copy.

88
00:04:36,447 --> 00:04:40,138
It supports one claim: these cases pass, at this revision.

89
00:04:40,481 --> 00:04:44,315
And it leaves evidence missing: the callers, the permissions,

90
00:04:44,315 --> 00:04:46,138
and the inputs nobody listed.

91
00:04:46,138 --> 00:04:50,537
Every observation has this shape: what you saw, the claim it supports,

92
00:04:50,537 --> 00:04:52,172
and what is still missing.

93
00:04:53,214 --> 00:04:57,625
Now take your own repository: your project, or the one you contribute to.

94
00:04:57,625 --> 00:05:00,164
First freeze a baseline at a named commit,

95
00:05:00,164 --> 00:05:03,185
and pick one small behavior an agent might change.

96
00:05:03,531 --> 00:05:06,620
You may ask an agent for a map and a list of commands.

97
00:05:06,620 --> 00:05:08,623
Each line of its answer is a claim.

98
00:05:08,623 --> 00:05:12,342
Verify it by opening the files and running the commands yourself.

99
00:05:12,681 --> 00:05:18,364
Then score what you observed, in four dimensions: structure, documentation,

100
00:05:18,364 --> 00:05:19,652
tests and checks.

101
00:05:20,697 --> 00:05:26,583
Each dimension has four levels, and each level has anchors: things you can observe.

102
00:05:26,583 --> 00:05:29,348
A level includes every anchor below it.

103
00:05:29,697 --> 00:05:33,613
Your score is the highest level whose anchors are all present.

104
00:05:33,613 --> 00:05:36,708
One missing anchor, and the score stops below it.

105
00:05:37,747 --> 00:05:38,466
Structure.

106
00:05:38,466 --> 00:05:43,930
Level three asks for three things: the map entries you checked are accurate,

107
00:05:43,930 --> 00:05:46,805
the change point has one responsibility,

108
00:05:46,805 --> 00:05:50,759
and your probe reaches it in three file opens or fewer.

109
00:05:50,759 --> 00:05:56,438
The evidence is a behavior, the files you opened in order, and a path and line.

110
00:05:56,781 --> 00:06:00,267
Say a session found the function in two file opens.

111
00:06:00,267 --> 00:06:04,505
That supports the map for this change point, at this revision.

112
00:06:04,505 --> 00:06:07,240
Other behaviors may have different maps.

113
00:06:07,240 --> 00:06:11,752
And one checked entry that turns out wrong would disprove a three.

114
00:06:12,797 --> 00:06:13,627
Documentation.

115
00:06:13,627 --> 00:06:17,479
At level three, every listed command runs at the scored revision,

116
00:06:17,479 --> 00:06:21,271
and at least three invariants name the checks that protect them.

117
00:06:21,271 --> 00:06:25,597
The evidence is the context file's path, each command with its exit code,

118
00:06:25,597 --> 00:06:27,848
and the list of invariants and checks.

119
00:06:28,197 --> 00:06:31,778
Say a copy lists three test commands, and two of them fail.

120
00:06:31,778 --> 00:06:34,935
Then documentation is a blocker for a fresh session.

121
00:06:34,935 --> 00:06:38,576
It says nothing about whether the implementation is correct.

122
00:06:38,576 --> 00:06:43,128
And one listed command that fails as written is enough to disprove a three.

123
00:06:44,164 --> 00:06:44,544
Tests.

124
00:06:44,544 --> 00:06:49,679
At level three, two repeatable runs agree, they stay within the budget you chose,

125
00:06:49,679 --> 00:06:53,166
they use no hidden input, and a deliberate break fails.

126
00:06:53,166 --> 00:06:57,223
The evidence is the two summaries, the search for hidden inputs,

127
00:06:57,223 --> 00:06:59,695
and the result of the deliberate break.

128
00:07:00,031 --> 00:07:01,554
What would disprove it?

129
00:07:01,554 --> 00:07:05,461
A run that passes while a deliberate break goes undetected.

130
00:07:05,461 --> 00:07:07,845
Or a test that reads a hidden input.

131
00:07:07,845 --> 00:07:12,547
So run the documented check twice, and inspect whether it uses a clock,

132
00:07:12,547 --> 00:07:14,402
the network or hidden files.

133
00:07:15,447 --> 00:07:15,883
Checks.

134
00:07:15,883 --> 00:07:19,619
At level three, one offline command runs the required gates,

135
00:07:19,619 --> 00:07:22,297
and it exits non-zero for an unused import.

136
00:07:22,297 --> 00:07:26,345
The evidence is the gate command, its failing and passing output,

137
00:07:26,345 --> 00:07:28,898
and the point where the gate is required.

138
00:07:29,247 --> 00:07:32,523
Say a hook rejects an unused import with exit two.

139
00:07:32,523 --> 00:07:35,799
That shows the hook can stop that class of change.

140
00:07:35,799 --> 00:07:39,402
It does not cover other checks, or the paths around it.

141
00:07:39,402 --> 00:07:43,858
And a gate you can run by hand, but that nothing requires, is a two.

142
00:07:44,896 --> 00:07:46,711
An agent may propose a score.

143
00:07:46,711 --> 00:07:47,588
You choose it.

144
00:07:47,588 --> 00:07:51,907
A number with no path, no revision and no output attached is a guess.

145
00:07:52,246 --> 00:07:57,255
So for each dimension, record five things: the path or command, the revision,

146
00:07:57,255 --> 00:08:02,004
the result you observed, the highest level whose anchors are all present,

147
00:08:02,004 --> 00:08:05,257
and one observation that would disprove the score.

148
00:08:06,296 --> 00:08:08,504
Your first score is a table of four rows.

149
00:08:08,504 --> 00:08:11,143
Now remove one blocker that is within your scope.

150
00:08:11,143 --> 00:08:13,351
For example, reconcile two test commands,

151
00:08:13,351 --> 00:08:15,667
or add a map from a behavior to its module.

152
00:08:16,013 --> 00:08:19,845
Then run the same probe at the new commit, and score again.

153
00:08:19,845 --> 00:08:21,664
The score may stay the same.

154
00:08:22,013 --> 00:08:26,154
A tidier directory, with no changed observation, does not raise a score.

155
00:08:26,154 --> 00:08:29,950
And if the same command now passes because its tests were deleted,

156
00:08:29,950 --> 00:08:32,424
keep the old score, and record the finding.

157
00:08:33,462 --> 00:08:35,306
So: is it ready for an agent?

158
00:08:35,306 --> 00:08:37,658
Don't answer from how the tree looks.

159
00:08:37,658 --> 00:08:41,091
A passing check is evidence for the inputs it covered.

160
00:08:41,091 --> 00:08:46,113
And a score changes only when the observed anchor changes, at a named revision.

161
00:08:46,462 --> 00:08:51,027
End your record with one decision: accept, narrow, recheck or stop.

162
00:08:51,027 --> 00:08:56,273
Name the evidence that supports it, and the observation that would change it.

episodes.title: Review before you ask
episodes.decision: write your own review of a change first. Then read a model's review as a list of hypotheses: mark each finding confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, with the evidence that disposition needs and, for cannot tell, the smallest next check. A review that reports nothing clears nothing, and the person with merge authority owns acceptance.

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:05,142
The rule: an account can edit a document exactly when it is active,

2
00:00:05,142 --> 00:00:07,291
and it is an owner or staff.

3
00:00:07,633 --> 00:00:09,998
Here is a course-written candidate.

4
00:00:09,998 --> 00:00:13,444
Check only an active staff account, and it behaves.

5
00:00:13,783 --> 00:00:15,794
But can an inactive owner edit?

6
00:00:16,833 --> 00:00:20,194
Write your own review before you ask a model.

7
00:00:20,194 --> 00:00:26,244
Python binds and more tightly than or, so this reads: owner, or staff and active.

8
00:00:26,583 --> 00:00:28,975
An owner alone makes it true.

9
00:00:28,975 --> 00:00:33,594
So an inactive owner can edit, and the contract says no.

10
00:00:33,933 --> 00:00:37,835
A review note names a location, an input, the expected result,

11
00:00:37,835 --> 00:00:41,045
the observed or traced result, and the consequence.

12
00:00:41,045 --> 00:00:43,184
Save that note before you read on.

13
00:00:44,233 --> 00:00:45,440
Then reproduce it.

14
00:00:45,440 --> 00:00:49,863
Inspect the supplied code, and run the public checks: seven tests.

15
00:00:49,863 --> 00:00:53,012
On the candidate, two fail: the inactive owner,

16
00:00:53,012 --> 00:00:56,564
and an inactive account that is both owner and staff.

17
00:00:56,900 --> 00:00:58,504
The run exits with one.

18
00:00:58,504 --> 00:01:01,991
Record your actual output, not a prediction of it.

19
00:01:03,033 --> 00:01:07,004
Now an agent proposes a revision: active, and owner or staff.

20
00:01:07,350 --> 00:01:09,511
That is still a proposal.

21
00:01:09,511 --> 00:01:15,045
Inspect the diff, apply only that expression in a separate copy,

22
00:01:15,045 --> 00:01:17,725
and rerun the unchanged checks.

23
00:01:17,725 --> 00:01:19,973
In our run all seven pass,

24
00:01:19,973 --> 00:01:25,161
and they cover the eight combinations of the three booleans.

25
00:01:25,500 --> 00:01:29,164
Could a lazier patch pass, one that denies everyone?

26
00:01:29,164 --> 00:01:29,376
No.

27
00:01:29,376 --> 00:01:31,631
In our run it fails three tests,

28
00:01:31,631 --> 00:01:36,071
the ones where an active owner or staff member must be allowed.

29
00:01:36,416 --> 00:01:38,152
And inspect the tests too.

30
00:01:38,152 --> 00:01:43,427
Changing what they expect, to fit the candidate, would not verify the contract.

31
00:01:44,465 --> 00:01:47,597
Only now, ask a model to review the same diff,

32
00:01:47,597 --> 00:01:50,933
with the contract and the exact files in context.

33
00:01:50,933 --> 00:01:53,316
Treat each comment as a hypothesis.

34
00:01:53,665 --> 00:01:56,793
A useful comment names a location and a check.

35
00:01:56,793 --> 00:01:59,036
A confident tone is not evidence.

36
00:01:59,382 --> 00:02:01,999
The model might catch the precedence bug.

37
00:02:01,999 --> 00:02:05,127
It might miss it, after seeing only a happy path.

38
00:02:05,127 --> 00:02:07,233
Or it might invent a requirement.

39
00:02:07,582 --> 00:02:08,836
And the order matters.

40
00:02:08,836 --> 00:02:11,058
If you read the model's comments first,

41
00:02:11,058 --> 00:02:13,793
agreeing with them is not an independent review.

42
00:02:14,832 --> 00:02:19,575
Here are three claims, written by the course to read like a model review.

43
00:02:19,575 --> 00:02:22,563
They are synthetic text, not a real model run.

44
00:02:22,899 --> 00:02:25,560
One: an inactive owner can edit.

45
00:02:25,560 --> 00:02:29,802
Two: parse the string false before deciding access.

46
00:02:29,802 --> 00:02:35,790
Three: a caller in another file relies on inactive owners being allowed.

47
00:02:36,132 --> 00:02:42,459
Every finding gets exactly one disposition: confirmed, refuted, or cannot tell.

48
00:02:42,459 --> 00:02:45,983
And each disposition needs its own evidence.

49
00:02:47,032 --> 00:02:50,830
Confirmed needs a reproducible input and an observed result,

50
00:02:50,830 --> 00:02:53,363
or a source trace that proves the claim.

51
00:02:53,698 --> 00:02:56,490
For claim one, we already have the input.

52
00:02:56,490 --> 00:03:00,234
Inactive, owner, not staff: the candidate returns true,

53
00:03:00,234 --> 00:03:02,549
and the inactive owner test fails.

54
00:03:02,549 --> 00:03:03,229
Confirmed.

55
00:03:03,565 --> 00:03:05,321
A comment can sound plausible.

56
00:03:05,321 --> 00:03:09,125
Without an input, a trace, or a check that fails and then passes,

57
00:03:09,125 --> 00:03:10,296
it is not confirmed.

58
00:03:11,330 --> 00:03:15,886
Refuted needs a check or a code reading that contradicts the claim,

59
00:03:15,886 --> 00:03:18,061
with the relevant input or line.

60
00:03:18,397 --> 00:03:22,016
Claim two asks the guard to parse the string false.

61
00:03:22,016 --> 00:03:27,337
But the contract takes booleans only, and so does the function's signature.

62
00:03:27,337 --> 00:03:29,040
The claim invents scope.

63
00:03:29,040 --> 00:03:29,608
Refuted.

64
00:03:30,646 --> 00:03:35,492
Claim three says a caller in another file relies on inactive owners being allowed.

65
00:03:35,492 --> 00:03:39,097
The function and the checks you were given contain no caller.

66
00:03:39,446 --> 00:03:42,006
It is tempting to call that refuted.

67
00:03:42,006 --> 00:03:47,337
But the files you have cannot answer it, so the disposition is cannot tell.

68
00:03:47,680 --> 00:03:51,077
Record three things: what you inspected, what is missing,

69
00:03:51,077 --> 00:03:53,998
and the smallest next check that would decide it.

70
00:03:53,998 --> 00:03:58,171
Here, you request the caller, and the behavior that was agreed for it.

71
00:03:59,212 --> 00:04:02,947
For each finding, run the smallest safe check you can explain.

72
00:04:02,947 --> 00:04:06,983
A model can suggest a test, but a person runs it and interprets it.

73
00:04:07,328 --> 00:04:13,154
Inspect any suggested command before you run it: its scope, its credentials,

74
00:04:13,154 --> 00:04:15,683
its network use, and its outputs.

75
00:04:15,683 --> 00:04:18,979
And keep the work in a dedicated directory.

76
00:04:20,028 --> 00:04:23,526
Suppose the model had reported only the string claim.

77
00:04:23,526 --> 00:04:25,969
It would have missed the real defect.

78
00:04:25,969 --> 00:04:29,599
So compare your first finding with every model comment,

79
00:04:29,599 --> 00:04:32,239
and keep any finding the model left out.

80
00:04:32,578 --> 00:04:35,156
And if the reviewer reports nothing at all?

81
00:04:35,156 --> 00:04:39,593
That says only that no finding was reported, for the context it was given.

82
00:04:39,593 --> 00:04:41,991
It does not prove the change is correct,

83
00:04:41,991 --> 00:04:45,109
or that a requirement nobody mentioned is satisfied.

84
00:04:45,445 --> 00:04:49,808
So keep a no-finding result beside three things: the scope the model saw,

85
00:04:49,808 --> 00:04:52,856
the checks you ran, and the cases it did not cover.

86
00:04:53,893 --> 00:04:55,636
So who accepts the change?

87
00:04:55,636 --> 00:05:00,864
In a repository pull request, the person with merge authority owns acceptance.

88
00:05:01,210 --> 00:05:06,334
The author owns a truthful handoff, and answers four questions: what changed, why,

89
00:05:06,334 --> 00:05:09,021
what could be wrong, and what was verified.

90
00:05:09,360 --> 00:05:13,584
A model, or another reviewer, supplies evidence and questions.

91
00:05:13,584 --> 00:05:15,491
Never an automatic approval.

92
00:05:15,827 --> 00:05:19,247
The decision is one of four: accept, narrow, recheck or stop.

93
00:05:19,247 --> 00:05:22,219
If the evidence is incomplete, it is recheck or stop,

94
00:05:22,219 --> 00:05:24,518
not an approval read off a green command.

95
00:05:25,560 --> 00:05:29,753
So: pin the base and the candidate, and write down the behavior.

96
00:05:29,753 --> 00:05:31,391
Review the diff yourself.

97
00:05:31,391 --> 00:05:35,715
Then ask the model, and keep its output apart from your own notes.

98
00:05:35,715 --> 00:05:36,960
Check each finding.

99
00:05:36,960 --> 00:05:40,891
And record the disposition, the evidence, and your decision.

100
00:05:41,226 --> 00:05:42,613
One question to try.

101
00:05:42,613 --> 00:05:47,534
A model says: the active staff example passes, so the guard is correct.

102
00:05:47,534 --> 00:05:50,515
Is that confirmed, refuted, or cannot tell?

103
00:05:50,515 --> 00:05:52,317
And which case is missing?

episodes.title: Would the tests notice?
episodes.decision: trust a green run only for the faults its tests could have noticed. A surviving mutant names the missing test. A property is only as wide as the inputs it covers, and its shrunk counterexample is kept as a regression. A patch that brings a survivor back has weakened the tests, whatever its hand-off says.

subtitles.en:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:02,330
A configuration field holds a level.

2
00:00:02,330 --> 00:00:05,437
Its contract is written before any code or test.

3
00:00:05,437 --> 00:00:10,228
It accepts exactly one digit, zero through nine, and returns that integer.

4
00:00:10,228 --> 00:00:13,011
Every other string must raise a ValueError.

5
00:00:13,350 --> 00:00:16,693
Here is a candidate parser, written to look reasonable.

6
00:00:16,693 --> 00:00:20,401
Give it three, and it returns three, so a first check passes.

7
00:00:20,750 --> 00:00:25,798
But a green run is evidence only for the faults its tests could have noticed.

8
00:00:25,798 --> 00:00:27,961
Would these tests notice a fault?

9
00:00:28,999 --> 00:00:30,896
The contract is the oracle.

10
00:00:30,896 --> 00:00:36,164
Every expected value comes from it, never from what the code happens to do.

11
00:00:36,164 --> 00:00:37,569
Three maps to three.

12
00:00:37,569 --> 00:00:40,730
The empty string and twelve must be rejected.

13
00:00:41,066 --> 00:00:45,406
Now predict which rejected inputs this code mishandles.

14
00:00:45,406 --> 00:00:50,298
For twelve, it reads only the first character and returns one.

15
00:00:50,298 --> 00:00:54,402
For the empty string, indexing raises an IndexError,

16
00:00:54,402 --> 00:00:57,637
where the contract requires a ValueError.

17
00:00:57,983 --> 00:00:59,272
Two distinct defects.

18
00:00:59,272 --> 00:01:02,343
And the candidate is correct on every valid input,

19
00:01:02,343 --> 00:01:04,554
so checks on valid inputs miss both.

20
00:01:05,598 --> 00:01:06,580
One trap first.

21
00:01:06,580 --> 00:01:11,031
Suppose an expected value is copied from what the candidate returns,

22
00:01:11,031 --> 00:01:13,257
so the test says twelve gives one.

23
00:01:13,257 --> 00:01:16,268
In our run, that test passes on the candidate,

24
00:01:16,268 --> 00:01:19,409
and fails on a parser that follows the contract.

25
00:01:19,748 --> 00:01:22,837
A wrong result equals the same wrong result.

26
00:01:22,837 --> 00:01:27,119
Give each expected value a source outside the implementation.

27
00:01:28,165 --> 00:01:32,645
Here is a test in the style an agent often produces when asked to "add tests".

28
00:01:32,645 --> 00:01:35,976
It calls the parser on three, then makes three assertions.

29
00:01:36,315 --> 00:01:38,390
Run it on the faulty candidate.

30
00:01:38,390 --> 00:01:42,406
Exit status zero: green, on code that violates its contract.

31
00:01:42,748 --> 00:01:44,918
Each assertion has a blind spot.

32
00:01:44,918 --> 00:01:47,087
The first is true for any value.

33
00:01:47,087 --> 00:01:50,206
The second only checks that a function exists.

34
00:01:50,206 --> 00:01:51,901
The third is always true.

35
00:01:51,901 --> 00:01:55,359
None of them compares the result with the contract.

36
00:01:56,398 --> 00:02:00,279
The unit checks state expected values: three for three,

37
00:02:00,279 --> 00:02:03,948
and a ValueError for the empty string, twelve and x.

38
00:02:03,948 --> 00:02:07,335
On the candidate, the run is red: an IndexError.

39
00:02:07,335 --> 00:02:13,191
That is a demonstrated defect: a known input, an expected result from the contract,

40
00:02:13,191 --> 00:02:15,449
and a different observed result.

41
00:02:15,798 --> 00:02:21,834
Generate: a repair is proposed, which checks the length before indexing.

42
00:02:21,834 --> 00:02:26,026
Verify: run the same, unchanged checks against it.

43
00:02:26,026 --> 00:02:26,529
Green.

44
00:02:26,865 --> 00:02:27,937
The order matters.

45
00:02:27,937 --> 00:02:31,393
You fix the intended behaviour and review the tests first.

46
00:02:31,393 --> 00:02:33,478
A person or an agent proposes code.

47
00:02:33,478 --> 00:02:35,504
An actual run judges the proposal.

48
00:02:35,504 --> 00:02:39,556
Now the harder question: which faults would these tests have missed?

49
00:02:40,598 --> 00:02:42,318
To find out, plant a fault.

50
00:02:42,318 --> 00:02:47,416
A mutant is a copy of a correct implementation with one small, deliberate fault.

51
00:02:47,416 --> 00:02:49,009
Run the suite against it.

52
00:02:49,348 --> 00:02:53,732
If a test fails, the mutant is killed: the suite noticed the fault.

53
00:02:53,732 --> 00:02:56,480
If every test passes, the mutant survived.

54
00:02:56,480 --> 00:03:00,799
The suite cannot see that change, or a real bug of the same shape.

55
00:03:01,148 --> 00:03:05,741
The fixture has three hand-written mutants of the repaired parser.

56
00:03:05,741 --> 00:03:08,734
One returns zero for every accepted string.

57
00:03:08,734 --> 00:03:10,891
One returns zero only for nine.

58
00:03:10,891 --> 00:03:14,719
One accepts trailing characters, so twelve returns one.

59
00:03:15,765 --> 00:03:18,702
Generate: suppose an agent proposes a first suite,

60
00:03:18,702 --> 00:03:21,521
with one accepted value and one rejected string.

61
00:03:21,521 --> 00:03:24,576
It reads well, and it passes on the repaired parser.

62
00:03:24,915 --> 00:03:27,254
Verify it by asking what it would notice.

63
00:03:27,254 --> 00:03:31,078
The run first requires the suite to pass on the unmutated original,

64
00:03:31,078 --> 00:03:32,390
then tries each mutant.

65
00:03:32,390 --> 00:03:33,646
It kills one of three.

66
00:03:33,981 --> 00:03:35,806
Read that as a list of gaps.

67
00:03:35,806 --> 00:03:39,065
One mutant survives because no test looks at nine.

68
00:03:39,065 --> 00:03:44,018
The other survives because the only rejected input, x, has no leading digit.

69
00:03:44,018 --> 00:03:49,232
Each survivor names the missing observation, so it tells you what test to write.

70
00:03:50,281 --> 00:03:52,657
So write exactly those tests.

71
00:03:52,657 --> 00:03:54,869
First: nine must give nine.

72
00:03:54,869 --> 00:03:59,212
That mutant is killed, and the count is two of three.

73
00:03:59,548 --> 00:04:01,836
Second: twelve must raise a ValueError.

74
00:04:01,836 --> 00:04:03,479
The last survivor is killed.

75
00:04:03,479 --> 00:04:04,359
Three of three.

76
00:04:04,698 --> 00:04:09,997
A new test earns its place when it fails on the mutant and passes on the original.

77
00:04:09,997 --> 00:04:13,229
A test that passes on both has not closed the gap.

78
00:04:14,264 --> 00:04:16,320
Four rules keep that count honest.

79
00:04:16,320 --> 00:04:18,376
One: the original must pass first.

80
00:04:18,376 --> 00:04:23,395
A suite that fails on the unmutated code "kills" everything, and has shown nothing.

81
00:04:23,731 --> 00:04:25,852
Two: state the denominator.

82
00:04:25,852 --> 00:04:31,431
"Three of three" means these three hand-written mutants, and no others.

83
00:04:31,431 --> 00:04:34,182
It does not prove the code correct.

84
00:04:34,531 --> 00:04:38,618
Three: a kill is a test failing because of the mutant's change.

85
00:04:38,618 --> 00:04:41,862
An import error or a broken harness is not a kill.

86
00:04:42,197 --> 00:04:46,474
Four: an equivalent mutant leaves the denominator, with a written reason.

87
00:04:46,474 --> 00:04:49,110
Change only the wording of the error message,

88
00:04:49,110 --> 00:04:51,512
and no test of this contract can kill it.

89
00:04:51,512 --> 00:04:55,027
But never drop a survivor that the contract can distinguish,

90
00:04:55,027 --> 00:04:56,608
just to improve the number.

91
00:04:57,646 --> 00:05:00,081
Examples check the inputs you thought of.

92
00:05:00,081 --> 00:05:04,178
A property is a statement that must hold for every input in a family,

93
00:05:04,178 --> 00:05:06,137
checked on many generated inputs.

94
00:05:06,479 --> 00:05:11,102
The first property people write here is a round trip over the ten valid values.

95
00:05:11,102 --> 00:05:13,091
On the faulty candidate it passes,

96
00:05:13,091 --> 00:05:16,250
